The Board

Ukraine, the Fed, and the Texas Grid

The war in Ukraine and the talks that follow it, the Federal Reserve's December decision and the debt-funded AI build behind it, and in Houston and Texas a new government waiting on institutions built to outlast it.

Scroll

Donetsk region

The front that will not move.

In October the army attacking it seized about 140 square kilometers and lost about 167. The war now runs on substations, calendars, and credit, and the trench is where all three land.

Photograph via NTB / document.dk. Ukrainian servicemen of the 24th Mechanized Brigade in a trench during training near the front line in Donetsk region. The front they hold has barely moved in a year of record effort.

What's Moved

Russia’s army net lost ground in October for the second straight month, while its strikes on Ukraine’s power grid widened west and grew heavier.

Abu Dhabi produced one thing: a prisoner exchange agreed in principle. It has not been carried out, and no number is final.

The European Commission proposed a 22nd sanctions package on November 23 and is preparing a new loan for Ukraine. Neither is adopted.

Markets rallied hard on Monday on reports that Jensen Huang had returned to Nvidia, after the worst week of the year. Bond yields did not follow the rally down.

Brent crude settled at $89.37 on Monday, its lowest since August, even as attacks on tankers near Hormuz were reported. Supply is beating fear.

In Texas, the outgoing administration’s regulators finalized the ERCOT chief’s contract through 2032, after the voters who fired them had already voted.

Verdict

Three boards moved this month, and on all three the event was not the power.

In Ukraine, Russia is losing ground slowly and raising the cost of winter quickly, and the talks reward the side that can wait.

In Washington, the Federal Reserve is set to raise rates into an AI build that its own customers increasingly finance on credit.

In Texas, voters replaced the government, and the appointed layer underneath it signed itself in through 2032 before the new one arrives.

The question this report answers is simple: who actually holds the leverage now, the people who won the event, or the institutions that were built to survive it?

Chapter One

The War on the Ground

Russia is losing ground slowly and raising the cost of winter quickly. The map and the grid are two different wars, and only one of them is moving.

On the night of November 23, Russia sent 96 drones at Ukraine. Ukraine said 73 were shot down or suppressed, and hits landed at 13 places.

That is now a normal night. It is also the whole war in one night: enormous effort, real damage, and no change in who holds what.

The Institute for the Study of War, which maps the front from geolocated footage, assessed that Russian forces net lost about 27 square kilometers in October.

They seized about 140 square kilometers and lost about 167. It was the second straight month of net loss.

The loss came in Donetsk, the province Russia says it must have. That is the sector Moscow calls its priority.

Fighting stays heaviest around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka, the towns guarding the Fortress Belt of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

On November 23 Ukraine’s General Staff counted 123 combat clashes in 22 hours, with 50 airstrikes and 171 guided bombs.

Russia can still generate that tempo. What it cannot do, on the mapped evidence, is turn tempo into ground.

Ukraine is striking the other way. Its drones have hit Russian refineries, pumping stations, and a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland in the past week alone.

The strikes are confirmed at named plants and pumping stations, from Novoshakhtinsk in Rostov to Tatarstan. What they have done to total Russian refining runs is not proven, and this report does not put a number on it.

The other war is the grid. Britain told the UN Security Council on November 23 that Russia launched 116 attacks on Ukrainian energy sites in the previous week.

One November attack left more than 600,000 people in Dnipropetrovsk region without power. Kyiv has run long daily outages through early November.

Substations are cheaper than infantry. A strike west of Kyiv raises the price of refusing Moscow’s terms without taking a single town.

That is the leverage. Russia does not need to win the map this winter. It needs Ukrainians cold, and negotiators in a hurry.

Chapter Two

The Talks and the Agenda

Abu Dhabi reopened a channel and produced a prisoner exchange in principle. On territory, guarantees, and the shape of the table, Moscow moved the agenda and Kyiv named its fallback.

The talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 were the first trilateral meeting since February. The United States sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

Russia sent Vladimir Medinsky. Ukraine sent Rustem Umerov. They left with a prisoner exchange agreed in principle and nothing else.

No ceasefire. No line. No agreement on territory, and strikes on the grid continued during the talks themselves.

What Moscow did win was the agenda. A wider European security order, its demand since 2021, is now a formal item for discussion.

Europe, whose money keeps Ukraine funded, was in side meetings. The Commission is preparing a further loan for 2027, not yet approved by member states.

Ukraine holds one new card. Its counter-drone teams are deployed across the Gulf, and other states are asking for the same help.

Kyiv’s price is pressure on Moscow. A cheap interceptor is becoming a diplomatic currency no one else can mint at scale.

Zelensky said on November 24 that the American envoys want a deal ideally by January 2027.

He also named his fallback. If the terms are not acceptable, Ukraine will go to the incoming Democratic-led Congress for more aid and tougher sanctions.

That deadline cuts both ways. Washington’s monopoly on the channel expires when Congress changes hands in January.

Russia knows the date too. Every week of grid strikes before January is meant to make Kyiv settle before its second channel opens.

On November 23 the Commission proposed a 22nd sanctions package, extending bans to about 60 more Russian banks.

A sanctions proposal is not a sanction. It needs every member state, and the last packages were held up for months.

Chapter Three

The Fed and the Price of Money

The committee held in October with both dissents asking for a hike. Jobs firmed, core prices ran at 0.3 percent for a third month, and December became a debate about size, not direction.

The Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time since July 2023. The target range is 3.75 to 4.00 percent.

In October it held, by 10 votes to 2. Both dissenters wanted a hike that day, which tells you the direction of the argument inside the room.

The minutes, released November 18, say almost all participants judged further increases would likely be appropriate.

One clause matters most. A couple of participants said a move larger than a quarter point could be warranted if inflation data came in hot.

October’s data then came in warm. Core consumer prices, stripping out food and energy, rose 0.3 percent for the third straight month.

There is no year-over-year October figure. The government collected no October 2025 prices during last year’s shutdown, so the comparison base does not exist.

Jobs argue the same way. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, and the two prior months were revised up by 84,000 combined.

The three-month average is now about 137,000. The labor market did not crack. It firmed.

Weekly jobless claims, the fastest honest layoff signal, were 203,000 in the week ending November 14. Firms are not firing.

Retail sales rose only 0.2 percent in October, but the control group that feeds the growth figures rose 0.6 percent.

Growth itself printed 3.4 percent annualized in the third quarter. Core PCE, the price measure the Fed actually targets, was 3.1 percent in September.

That is the case the committee will carry into December 8 and 9. It will decide before it sees November’s consumer prices, which arrive December 10.

New York Fed President John Williams said on November 23 that inflation is too high and returning it to 2 percent is essential.

He did not rule out moving at consecutive meetings. The next data test is tomorrow, when October PCE is released.

Governor Christopher Waller set the test for a larger move in advance. If October core inflation came in at 0.3 percent or higher, he said, a half-point hike should be considered.

It came in at exactly 0.3 percent. That is why December is a debate about size, not direction.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned on November 22 that the Fed could make a policy mistake by tightening too far.

The market heard him and kept pricing a December hike anyway. Public pressure from the Treasury is not a vote on the committee.

Chapter Four

The Build and Its Credit

Nvidia's demand is real and its financing is circular: the seller guarantees the buyers' credit while the central bank raises its price. The physical tells refuse to call it a boom.

Monday showed what this market now rests on. The S&P 500 rose 4.7 percent in a day, its best since April 2025.

The driver was one company. Nvidia rose about 31 percent on reports that Jensen Huang, who resigned on November 12, had returned, adding roughly $950 billion in market value. The full telling of the resignation is in Coffee to Kalshi; here it matters only as the trigger.

The week before, the same index fell 8.6 percent. A market that moves like this on one name is telling you where its weight sits.

Seven stocks made up about 33 percent of the S&P 500 at the start of November. The index is a concentrated bet wearing a diversified label.

Nvidia’s numbers, reported November 17, are real. Revenue was $115.8 billion in the quarter, up 103 percent from a year earlier.

Data centers brought in $107.6 billion of that. The next quarter is guided to about $130 billion, assuming no data center sales to China.

The financing underneath is the story. Nvidia’s supply and capacity commitments jumped to $390 billion in one quarter, from $279 billion.

Its maximum guarantee exposure is $118 billion. That includes credit support tied to a data center campus in Ohio, for customers who need the support to borrow.

The four big buyers are spending at the same pace. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta spent $201.9 billion on property and equipment in the third quarter alone.

That was up 108 percent from a year earlier, and more than their operating cash flow for the quarter. The gap is debt.

Put the two halves together. The seller guarantees the buyers’ credit, the buyers borrow to buy, and the central bank raises the price of the borrowing.

None of that makes the demand fake. It makes the demand conditional, in a way it was not when the build ran on cash flow.

The physical tells refuse to confirm a boom. Brent has fallen about 24 percent in a month, on returning supply from Libya and the Middle East.

Hormuz clearance ran at only about 42 percent of pre-war levels in early November, on Kpler’s count, and attacks on tankers were reported on Monday. Oil fell anyway.

The dollar hit a 19-month high on Monday. Capital is paying up for dollars and for a 10-year Treasury yield near 4.9 percent at the same time.

That is tightening, not easing, whatever one stock did on Monday. The rally changed a price. It did not change the cost of money.

Chapter Five

Houston

Houston first. The mayor's calendar strategy on immigration, a tabled county money fight, a sheriff writing surveillance rules alone, and a $4.4 billion sale that lands on a Houston balance sheet.

Houston’s mayor is spending his post-election leverage early, and his main weapon is the calendar.

On November 6, John Whitmire ordered Houston police to contact federal immigration agents only when a person is already being arrested for a jailable offense and a federal database hit shows an immigration warrant.

Attorney General Ken Paxton asked a Fort Bend County court to rule that the order violates SB 4, the 2017 state law on immigration enforcement.

The city’s own attorney told the council that writing the same order into law would be unlawful under SB 4.

He also said, in public, that it will be hard for Paxton to get a ruling before the new state administration takes over in January.

That is the strategy stated plainly. The order does not need to win in court. It needs to outlast the plaintiff.

Whitmire is also building a bloc. He has met the other big-city Texas mayors this month about a joint push for state funding and room to govern.

The constraint has not moved. Republicans still hold the Texas Senate, and every city ask needs votes from that chamber.

At the county, nothing was settled. Commissioners tabled the fight over $180 million in toll road mobility money on November 12.

The 2025 formula stands, and it gives the largest share to Precinct 3. Rodney Ellis has tied his future budget vote to changing it.

The Port did not move this week. Its November 10 budget, a $569 million operating plan and a $397 million capital plan, stands as adopted, and the commission meets again on December 8.

One Houston decision did land. The sheriff rewrote the county’s license plate reader rules, in a policy revised November 20 and reported November 23.

The office runs 480 cameras across 20 networks. Historical searches now need a detective’s rank, a case number, and a reason tied to a suspected crime.

Plate data must be destroyed 30 days after collection unless it sits in a case file. The sheriff wrote the rule alone and can rewrite it alone.

Houston money moved in one clean line. ConocoPhillips, headquartered here, agreed on November 23 to sell its Norway business to Vår Energi.

The stated consideration is $4.4 billion, with about $2.5 billion in net cash expected. It ends a North Sea presence that began with the Ekofisk discovery in 1969.

The leverage point is where the cash lands. A Houston balance sheet gets lighter and more liquid while the city’s other big energy bet, the grid build, gets more expensive to finance.

Chapter Six

Texas

Then Texas. A new government elected on November 3 waits until January, while the outgoing one's appointees sign the grid chief in through 2032 and the data center queue awaits its December audit.

Texas voted on November 3 to replace its government. Democrats won the governor’s office, the other statewide offices, and the state House, 83 seats to 67.

Republicans kept the state Senate, 19 seats to 12. That one hold is the difference between a new government and a new argument.

The legislature convenes on January 12. The governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, is sworn in on January 19. Until then, the old administration governs.

It used the window on the grid. Regulators finalized ERCOT chief Pablo Vegas’s new contract on November 19 and 20, after the election.

The contract runs from January 2027 through 2032. His base pay is about $1.16 million a year, with incentives that could take the six-year total to $29.5 million at most.

In 2027 the most he can actually be paid is about $4.1 million. The big number is a ceiling over six years, not a salary.

Dan Patrick, who lost the lieutenant governor’s race, called himself disgusted and said he was not notified. Hinojosa called the decision the outgoing administration’s.

Neither reaction changes the document. A contract signed by an appointed board outlasts an election in a way a statute does not.

The same insulation is being tested on data centers. ERCOT has not approved energizing any new data center or crypto load of 75 megawatts or more since August 3.

About 474 gigawatts of large-load requests sat in the queue in June. Those are requests, not demand, and not plants. Most will never be built.

In September, ERCOT’s first sorting of a roughly 496 gigawatt universe excluded about 302 gigawatts of it. Its verification report is due December 10, and the utilities commission takes it up December 17.

CenterPoint, meanwhile, raised its ten-year capital plan to $70.7 billion in October. It expects 14 gigawatts of new demand in greater Houston by 2030.

Both numbers can be true at once. The queue is paper. The Houston load growth underneath it is steel, wire, and signed customers.

Houston also holds the Speaker’s chair, if the pledges hold. Rep. Senfronia Thompson of Houston says she has 90 pledges, 14 more than she needs.

The governor-elect’s transition is run by Joe Madden, formerly chief of staff to Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo.

That is a Houston pipeline into Austin that has not existed in decades. It runs through committee chairs and appointments, not speeches.

Chapter Seven

Two Rival Reads

Was November a month when institutions beat events, or the month the events lined up their dates? Two coherent answers, and the evidence that separates them.

Read One: Control Beat the Events The strongest case for this read is that every November event failed to move the layer underneath it.

Russia lost ground and still set the negotiating agenda. The Fed’s critics spoke and pricing hardened anyway. Nvidia’s founder crisis came and went inside a financing structure that did not change.

Texas is the cleanest proof. Voters fired the administration, and its appointees signed the grid chief in for six more years within the month.

On this read, power lives in contracts, committees, queues, and calendars. Elections and headlines are weather. The institutions are the climate.

This read answers the strongest evidence against it directly. The Senate hold, the contract, and the unexecuted prisoner exchange are not details. They are the record.

Read Two: The Events Are Compounding The strongest case for this read is that the events have dates, and the dates are close together.

Ukraine’s second channel in Congress opens in January. The Fed decides on December 9. ERCOT reports on December 10, and the Texas legislature convenes on January 12.

Each date converts an event into a decision someone must take in public, with a vote or a signature attached.

Russia’s grid campaign also cuts this way. It is an admission that the front cannot deliver what Moscow wants before those dates arrive.

This read meets the strongest evidence against it directly. Insulation works only until a legislature, a court, or a financing failure reaches the insulated layer, and all three are now scheduled.

Chapter Eight

Scenarios

Three futures with triggers that separate them. A trigger that stays true either way is not a trigger, and none of these is presented as certain.

Scenario One: A freeze built on the grid. Talks produce an executed prisoner exchange by mid-December and a second round with Europeans seated. Confirm it with named lists and a dated exchange. Kill it if the exchange stays in principle while substation strikes continue into the December cold.

Scenario Two: The Fed goes 50. October PCE, out tomorrow, prints hot enough that the larger move Waller described becomes the committee’s credibility test. Confirm it with a core PCE reading well above September’s 3.1 percent. Kill it with a soft PCE print and a soft December 4 jobs report together.

Scenario Three: The queue gets cut in public. ERCOT’s December 10 report validates only a small share of the requested load, and the financing story reprices with it. Confirm it with a cut of more than half the queued gigawatts. Kill it if the report validates more than 100 gigawatts as real, dated projects.

Chapter Nine

Watchlist

Five developments that would change the analysis.

1. The prisoner exchange. If it executes with lists and dates by mid-December, Abu Dhabi was a channel. If it slips, it was an announcement.

2. October PCE on November 25, then the December 4 jobs report. Together they set whether December 9 is a quarter point or a fight over 50.

3. ERCOT’s December 10 verification report and the December 17 commission meeting. This is where paper demand becomes, or fails to become, Texas load.

4. OPEC+ on November 29. A cartel that cannot lift Brent off three-month lows, with supply returning, has less leverage than its communiqués claim.

5. A Fort Bend ruling on Houston’s immigration order before January. A ruling for Paxton inverts the city’s calendar strategy in a day.
